namespace Erdos164

/--
A set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ is primitive if no member of $A$ divides another. Is the sum
$$\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n\log n}$$
maximised over all primitive sets when $A$ is the set of primes?

Erdős [Er35] proved that this sum always converges for a primitive set. Lichtman [Li23] proved
that the answer is yes. An alternative, simpler, proof is given by Alexeev, Barreto, Li, Lichtman,
Price, Shah, Tang, and Tao [ABLLPSTT26].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/1d7b3f00780b85ed0462e79a1cd5650ee9055655/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos164.lean"]
theorem erdos_164 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ A : Set ℕ, (∀ a ∈ A, 2 ≤ a) → Erdos1196.IsPrimitive A →
      (∑' a : A, 1 / ((a : ℕ) * Real.log (a : ℕ))) ≤
        ∑' p : {p : ℕ | p.Prime}, 1 / ((p : ℕ) * Real.log (p : ℕ)) := by
  sorry

end Erdos164

reformulations.difference: The maximization question is expressed as a universal upper bound, and the imported primitive predicate uses association rather than explicitly forbidding divisibility between distinct elements.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: On ℕ, Associated x y is equivalent to x = y, since 1 is the only unit. Thus IsPrimitive is exactly the required divisibility-antichain condition. The restriction 2 ≤ a matches Lichtman's domain of integers greater than 1. The prime set satisfies both hypotheses, so its objective value belongs to the feasible values; the universal upper bound is therefore equivalent to that value being their greatest element. Both the primitive-predicate equivalence and the full maximum reformulation were proved in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: The inequality uses real-valued tsum without separately asserting convergence.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Erdős's cited convergence theorem already ensures the intended meaning. Independently, the universal inequality itself forces summability: every finite subset of an admissible primitive set remains admissible and primitive, so its finite weight sum is bounded by the same real constant. All weights are nonnegative, hence bounded finite sums imply summability. The primes are also admissible. Consequently, the theorem is equivalent to the formulation with an explicit Summable assertion, not a weaker statement exploiting tsum's default zero. This equivalence was proved in Lean for an arbitrary real upper bound.
